analysis.one_liner: Restores federal Clean Water Act protections to all streams, wetlands, and ponds, not just navigable waters.
analysis.headline: The Senate committee held one hearing but never voted on a bill to restore federal pollution protections to small streams and wetlands, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: After a 2006 Supreme Court ruling narrowed the Clean Water Act to only 'navigable waters,' millions of small streams, wetlands, and ponds lost federal pollution protections. This bill replaced that term with 'waters of the United States,' putting small and intermittent streams, wetlands, and prairie potholes back under the EPA and Army Corps permit system. It kept existing exemptions for normal farming, ranching, and certain stormwater runoff. The bill drew 22 Senate backers, got one committee hearing, and then went nowhere: the committee never voted it out, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people whose drinking water comes from streams and wetlands — the bill's findings state that source-water areas with small or intermittent streams supply more than 110 million Americans [S3]. Also the tens of millions who fish, hunt, and recreate on inland waters, and communities downstream of industrial and sewage discharges that would again need permits. Clean-water safeguards reduce treatment costs and flood damage that otherwise fall on local taxpayers and homeowners [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drinking-water customers, anglers, and flood-prone communities

how_it_helps.text: Small and intermittent streams make up the majority of stream miles in the U.S. and feed and purify drinking water supplies serving more than 110 million Americans; the bill brings them back under federal pollution controls.
Wetlands and streams absorb floodwaters; the findings state that draining or filling them causes billions of dollars in flood damage annually, so restoring oversight protects flood-prone communities.

More than 14,000 industrial plants and municipal sewage systems discharge into small or intermittent streams; replacing 'navigable waters' with 'waters of the United States' puts all of those discharges back under permit requirements.
Fishing, hunting, and water-based recreation that depend on these waters generate hundreds of billions of dollars a year for tourism and sporting businesses, which benefit from cleaner water.

analysis.who_pays: Developers, homebuilders, and industrial or municipal dischargers who fill wetlands or discharge into small streams, because they would need federal permits for work that the narrowed rules had left unchecked. Some landowners face permit costs and delay even though the bill explicitly preserves exemptions for normal farming, ranching, and drainage-ditch maintenance [S3].

drawbacks.text: The definition reaches all intrastate waters — including natural ponds, prairie potholes, wet meadows, and intermittent streams — which would put many activities on private land under federal permitting and raised genuine property-rights and federalism objections.

Even with the savings clause, landowners and developers would face more permit requirements, delay, and cost for any work affecting protected waters, and the line between an exempt 'normal farming' discharge and a regulated one can be hard to draw in practice.
The bill clarifies jurisdiction but appropriates no new money for wastewater treatment or monitoring, so expanded rules could land on state agencies and permit applicants without added resources.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is large: the bill would restore pollution and fill permits for the small streams and wetlands that feed the drinking water supplies of more than 110 million Americans, filter pollutants, and buffer floods [S3]. The costs are real but narrower: broader federal permitting would mean more paperwork and delay for developers, road builders, and landowners, and even with the farming exemptions in the savings clause, some agricultural land uses could face new oversight [S3]. The bill also deliberately carried no new money for water infrastructure — it was a jurisdictional fix, not a funding bill. On balance it was a genuine public-health and environmental protection whose main flaw was drafting the federal reach so broadly that it guaranteed a political fight it never survived.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee, and got one hearing — but the committee never voted to send it to the Senate floor, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 25, 2007 and read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.
The committee held hearings on April 9, 2008 (printed as S.Hrg. 110-1245), but no markup or floor vote followed.
No further action was taken before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, so the bill died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Developers, industrial dischargers, and other polluters who would have needed permits to fill or discharge into small streams and wetlands were better off, since the regulatory gap left by the court decision stayed open. Homeowners and communities that drink from or live near those waters paid the price in continued exposure to unregulated discharges.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Developers and dischargers who avoided permits

for.name: Russell Feingold
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led the effort to redefine Clean Water Act jurisdiction after the 2006 Supreme Court ruling narrowed it.

for.name: 19 of 49 Senate Democrats (plus one Independent and one Independent Democrat)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it 22 total backers in the Senate.

for.name: Barbara Boxer
for.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
for.what_they_did: As committee chair and a cosponsor, presided over the April 2008 hearings on the bill, but the committee never reported it out.

against.name: National Association of Home Builders, farm organizations, and mining interests
against.role: Industry coalitions opposed to expanded Clean Water Act jurisdiction
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against the bill as an unprecedented expansion of federal permitting over private land, streams, and ponds.

against.name: Bush administration
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill as an overbroad expansion of federal water jurisdiction beyond the constitutional power claimed for it.

against.name: James Inhofe
against.role: Ranking Member, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill in committee as a federal overreach into state and private water management.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 Senate backers were Democrats, an Independent, and an Independent Democrat; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill never reached a floor vote where party counts could be recorded.

industries.note: Filling wetlands or building across small streams and ponds would again require federal permits under the Clean Water Act, adding cost, delay, and limits to projects on land the bill newly covers. That cost is the flip side of flood and water protection for nearby communities.

The savings clause keeps the existing exemptions for normal farming, ranching, irrigation return flows, and drainage-ditch maintenance [S3], so routine farm work stays off the hook — but farms near newly covered waters could still face oversight for non-routine discharges.

Precipitation-only stormwater runoff from oil, gas, and mining operations keeps its existing exemption [S3], but mines and well sites near intermittent streams lose the regulatory gap the court decision opened for other discharges.

industries.industry: Water utilities and municipal sewage systems
industries.note: Discharges into small streams would be clearly federally regulated again, which for utilities means clearer permits; downstream drinking water sources stay better protected, lowering treatment burdens.
